cards.front: Recall a key point about Chromatography
cards.back: Chromatography is a separation technique used to separate the components of a mixture. It works because different substances have different solubilities in the same solvent, so they travel at different rates through the stationary phase.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Chromatography
cards.back: Chromatography has two phases: Mobile phase — the solvent that moves through the paper (e.g. water or ethanol). Stationary phase — the material that does not move (e.g. chromatography paper). Components that are more soluble in the mobile phase travel faster and further. Components that are more attracted to the stationary phase travel slower and stay closer to the origin.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Chromatography
cards.back: Follow these steps to carry out paper chromatography: Draw a pencil baseline near the bottom of the chromatography paper. Never use ink — it would dissolve and run. Place small spots of each sample on the baseline using a capillary tube. Place the paper in a beaker containing a small amount of solvent . The solvent level must be below the baseline. Cover the beaker with a lid to prevent evaporation and keep the atmosphere saturated with solvent vapour. Allow the solvent to rise up the paper by capillary action . cards.front: Recall a key point about Chromatography
cards.back: The result is a chromatogram — a pattern of spots showing where each component has moved to on the paper.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Chromatography
cards.back: The Rf value is always between 0 and 1 . A substance with an Rf value close to 1 is very soluble in the mobile phase and travels almost as far as the solvent front. A substance with an Rf value close to 0 is barely soluble and stays near the baseline.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Chromatography
cards.back: The Rf value of a substance is constant for a given solvent at a given temperature. This means you can compare Rf values to identify unknown substances by matching them against known reference values.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Chromatography
cards.back: Changing the solvent changes the Rf values because the solubility of each component changes. If a substance does not move in one solvent, try a different solvent.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Chromatography
cards.back: When interpreting a chromatogram: A pure substance produces a single spot on the chromatogram. A mixture produces two or more spots , because the different components separate out. Two substances are likely the same compound if they produce spots at the same height (same Rf value) when run on the same chromatogram. If a spot from a known reference is at the same position as a spot from an unknown sample, the unknown likely contains that substance.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Chromatography
cards.back: Sometimes different substances have the same Rf value in one solvent, so they do not separate properly. Two-way chromatography (also called two-dimensional chromatography) solves this problem by using two different solvents at right angles to each other.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Chromatography
cards.back: Method for two-way chromatography: Carry out chromatography in the first solvent as normal. Allow the paper to dry completely. Turn the paper 90 degrees so the baseline is now vertical on one side. Run chromatography again using a different solvent . Components that did not separate in the first solvent may now separate in the second solvent because they have different solubilities.

cards.front: What does Type of solvent mean?
cards.back: Different solvents give different Rf values for the same substance. Choose a solvent that gives good separation.
Rf values change with temperature because solubility changes. Always compare Rf values obtained at the same temperature.
